endpoints.interpretation: Fluoride ion release and defluorination fraction were measured to assess the extent of PFOA defluorination during regeneration of PFOA-preloaded resins by SR-AOP at 10 mM PDS and other regeneration routes in feasibility tests.
Decrease of sorbed PFOA and destruction of PFOA structure during SR-AOP regeneration was used to evaluate detoxification of resin-bound PFOA.
Recovery of PFOA adsorption capacity of the ion exchange resin after SR-AOP regeneration was used as an indicator of successful resin regeneration.

limitations.statement: Feasibility tests at 10 mM PDS and other routes were conducted on PFOA-preloaded resins in ultrapure water, which may not represent performance in more complex water matrices.
The study focused on a single PFAS (PFOA), limiting generalizability to other PFAS chemistries.

comparability.reason: This record describes cyclic IX adsorption with SR-AOP regeneration at a specific PDS dose (30 mM) and over a defined number of cycles, including qualitative statements about capacity recovery and resin damage, but lacks quantitative removal percentages or directly comparable capacity metrics under standardized conditions.

endpoints.interpretation: Cumulative removal of PFOA from aqueous solution over successive IX adsorption cycles with regeneration at 30 mM PDS was evaluated to demonstrate the cyclic treatment performance; cumulative PFOA removal increased linearly with cycle number for regenerated resins.
Destruction of PFOA sorbed on the resins during SR-AOP regeneration at 30 mM PDS was used to demonstrate detoxification of the concentrated PFOA on the resin.
Fluoride ion release and defluorination fraction were monitored during regeneration to assess the extent of PFOA defluorination.

Recovery of PFOA adsorption capability after each regeneration cycle at 30 mM PDS was used as a functional endpoint for resin regeneration; authors report that regeneration with a low PDS dose effectively recovered adsorption capability with only slight resin destruction.

Resin morphology and structure were evaluated by SEM, EDS, and FTIR after six cycles at 30 mM PDS; several cracks appeared on the resin surface at the 6th cycle but the surface mostly remained complete, indicating limited material damage at this PDS dose.

limitations.statement: The cyclic adsorption–regeneration experiments were performed under controlled laboratory conditions with a single PFOA contaminant, which may not reflect behavior in complex natural or wastewaters or when multiple PFAS are present.
Only up to six adsorption–regeneration cycles were evaluated for resin performance and damage at 30 mM PDS, limiting understanding of long-term durability beyond six cycles.

comparability.reason: This record characterizes performance and material integrity of ion exchange resins under a high PDS dose (300 mM) but does not provide directly comparable quantitative capacity or removal metrics relative to lower-dose conditions; evidence is mainly qualitative regarding damage and capacity loss.

endpoints.interpretation: Cumulative PFOA removal over cycles was assessed for resins regenerated at 300 mM PDS, but high oxidant dose led to serious damage and irreversible loss of adsorption capacity despite PFOA degradation.
Destruction of PFOA sorbed on the resins occurred during SR-AOP regeneration at 300 mM PDS, contributing to detoxification, but resin functionality deteriorated.
At 300 mM PDS, severe resin material damage caused irreversible loss in adsorption capacity, indicating that this high oxidant dose is unsuitable for sustainable resin regeneration.

limitations.statement: High PDS dose experiments (300 mM) were conducted at bench scale and primarily aimed at mechanistic understanding of resin damage, not at process optimization for practical systems.
The study did not report quantitative adsorption capacity values or removal percentages after each cycle at 300 mM PDS, limiting direct comparison of performance loss over time.

comparability.reason: The study reports qualitative or relative regeneration performance (e.g., near-complete PFAS desorption, more bed volumes required for PFAS-selective resins) under different regenerant compositions and bed volumes, but does not provide consistent quantitative desorption percentages or capacity recovery values in the supplied excerpts needed for direct comparison across conditions.

endpoints.interpretation: PFAS were desorbed from loaded anion exchange resins into regenerant brine/cosolvent solutions. Conventional regenerable AERs achieved near-complete PFAS desorption with 10 bed volumes of 70% methanolic brine, while PFAS-selective resins required 30 bed volumes of higher methanol content (90%) or more hydrophobic cosolvent (n-propanol) brines. The endpoint is PFAS transfer from solid resin to liquid regenerant, enabling resin reuse rather than PFAS destruction.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS desorption and resin regeneration efficacy

limitations.statement: Continuous-flow regeneration required substantially more bed volumes of regenerant for PFAS-selective resins (30 BVs of high-cosolvent brine) than for conventional regenerable AERs (10 BVs of 70% methanolic brine), which implies larger regenerant volumes and associated waste streams for PFAS-selective media.

Site-specific pilot testing is recommended to ensure optimum PFAS treatment and regeneration performance prior to full-scale implementation, due to potential influences of matrix components such as dissolved iron and manganese scaling.

Emerging liquid-phase PFAS destruction technologies such as hydrothermal alkaline treatment, electrochemical oxidation, plasma treatment, and supercritical water oxidation have high energy requirements (>100 kWh/m3), so concentrating PFAS into a small regenerant waste volume is advantageous before destruction.

endpoints.interpretation: The batch experiments measured PFAS desorption from resins into regenerant solutions as an indicator of regeneration efficacy. Combined salt brine and organic cosolvent mixtures were necessary for effective desorption, with performance dependent on salt type and cosolvent composition. The outcome represents improved phase transfer of PFAS from solid resin to liquid regenerant, not PFAS degradation.

limitations.statement: Neither brine-only nor solvent-only regenerant solutions led to effective PFAS desorption, indicating that combined ionic strength and cosolvent effects are required for regeneration of both conventional and PFAS-selective AERs.

Little is known regarding the efficiency of methanol distillation from varied regenerant solution matrices and the potential for PFAS back-contamination due to volatility, highlighting uncertainty in resource recovery performance.

records.citation: Chiang, S.Y.D.; Saba, M.; Leighton, M.; Ballenghien, D.; Hatler, D.; Gal, J.; Deshusses, M.A. Supercritical water oxidation for the destruction of spent media wastes generated from PFAS treatment. Journal of Hazardous Materials. 2023, 460, 132264.

comparability.reason: Bench-/pilot-scale continuous SCWO treatment of slurried PFAS-laden GAC from full-scale water treatment, reporting total PFAS loading and qualitative destruction/mineralization outcomes under supercritical conditions; generally comparable to other records from the same study that treat AIX spent media under similar SCWO conditions.

endpoints.interpretation: Authors describe SCWO as very effective for destruction of PFAS adsorbed on spent GAC, based on large reductions of target PFAS in effluent streams after treatment.

Authors report that spent GAC media were completely mineralized to water, CO2 and a negligible amount of residual minerals. This refers mainly to the carbonaceous media matrix; PFAS mineralization is inferred but fluoride balance was not quantified in this study.

Defluorination/mineralization of organofluorine was not directly quantified because inorganic fluoride increases from complete PFAS mineralization were below detection against background fluoride; thus defluorination is not confirmed by a fluoride mass balance in this study.

limitations.statement: Fluoride mass balance and PFAS destruction were not evaluated via inorganic fluoride measurements because complete mineralization would only increase fluoride by about 0.06 mg/L, which could not be measured accurately over background.
Authors state that a longer-term study and full mass balance of PFAS and fluorine in SCWO system outputs are needed to confirm destruction and mineralization for spent media.
SCWO system used was originally designed for less recalcitrant wastes and was not redesigned specifically for PFAS elimination, which may limit optimization for PFAS destruction.

Energy consumption, air quality impacts, carbon footprint, and life cycle assessment are needed to compare SCWO with current PFAS waste management practices such as incineration, deep well injection, and landfilling.
Study treats discrete samples of spent media in a SCWO system; full-scale commercial systems able to treat entire volumes from filtration vessels are still needed to validate findings at scale.

limitations.statement: Regeneration of the anion exchange resins was not experimentally performed in this field pilot; media usage rates and regeneration implications are inferred from breakthrough behavior and conceptual criteria for changeout/regeneration.

Results reflect a single groundwater site with elevated PFAS concentrations (> 10 µg/L) and specific mixture composition and geochemistry, which the authors note can significantly influence breakthrough and media usage rates.

Comparison between regenerable and single-use resins is based on breakthrough and modeled bed volumes to specified criteria, not on measured regeneration efficiency, capacity recovery, or multi-cycle performance.

Results are site-specific to one groundwater with elevated PFAS concentrations and particular mixture composition and may not directly extrapolate to lower-concentration or compositionally different sites.

records.citation: Ling, A. L.; Vermace, R. R.; McCabe, A. J.; Wolohan, K. M.; Kyser, S. J. Is removal and destruction of perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances from wastewater treatment plant effluent affordable and feasible? Water Environment Research. 2024, 96, e10975. DOI: 10.1002/wer.10975.

comparability.reason: The study provides modeled breakthrough behavior, O&M cost multipliers, and qualitative rules for routing PFAS-loaded GAC to reactivation versus HTI under specific WRRF-scale design and regulatory assumptions. It does not report empirical regeneration efficiencies, capacity recovery over cycles, or destruction efficiencies, so results are best used qualitatively to inform relative costs of media replacement versus reactivation/incineration rather than quantitatively compared with laboratory adsorption–regeneration experiments.

endpoints.interpretation: Modeled separation of PFAS from WRRF effluent by GAC/AIX adsorbers, characterized by time or bed volumes to breakthrough at 5 ng/L, used to estimate media usage and O&M costs.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS removal effectiveness; breakthrough time; bed volumes to breakthrough

endpoints.interpretation: End-of-life destruction of PFAS-loaded sorption media through GAC reactivation or HTI is included as a necessary step to prevent environmental release and is incorporated into lifecycle cost estimates; no experimental destruction efficiency is reported.
endpoints.reported_term: Destruction of PFAS on spent media via GAC reactivation or high-temperature incineration (HTI)

endpoints.interpretation: Modeled operational and maintenance cost multipliers for treating short-chain PFAS relative to C8 PFAS, and assessment of household cost impacts and affordability of adding PFAS separation and destruction to WRRFs.
endpoints.reported_term: O&M cost multipliers and affordability of WRRF PFAS treatment

limitations.statement: Modeling is based on assumed influent PFBA and PFBS concentrations, simplified breakthrough criteria (5 ng/L), and statewide average conditions; authors note substantial design uncertainties and the need for full-scale testing to ensure consistent PFAS removal and destruction at WRRFs.

Temporal variability in PFAS loading to WRRFs (requiring up to nine daily grab samples for characterization in other work) limits accuracy of media changeout frequency predictions and complicates compliance with low-level PFAS effluent limits.

Cost and design assumptions for media destruction focus only on two technologies currently available at WRRF-relevant scale (GAC reactivation and HTI); other destruction options may emerge with different capital and O&M costs.

The analysis assumes that GAC from facilities with design flowrates >1 MGD will be sent to site-dedicated reactivation, while smaller facilities use HTI; this threshold is based on vendor discussions and may not reflect all market conditions.

Results represent facilities with minimal industrial PFAS inputs; WRRFs with significant industrial PFAS loads may need more frequent media changeout and/or additional vessels, increasing capital and O&M costs beyond modeled ranges.
